content: {"summary":"To verify whether PostgreSQL is still serving the old certificate, compare the certificate presented by the server with the file on disk using openssl; if the serial numbers differ, the server is using the old cert. Reload the PostgreSQL configuration (SELECT pg_reload_conf() or systemctl reload) to make it load the renewed files. The replica (auth-db-02) has its own certificate and timer and must be reloaded in the same way.","likely_cause":"PostgreSQL has not reloaded its configuration after the certificate was renewed, so it continues to present the previous certificate.","confidence":"high","claims":[{"text":"Compare the server's presented certificate with the on‑disk file to detect a mismatch","evidence_ids":["RB-024#2"],"quote":"Compare what the server sends with what is on disk:"},{"text":"Reload PostgreSQL configuration to make it load the new certificate without a full restart","evidence_ids":["RB-024#2"],"quote":"Reload, don't restart: SELECT pg_reload_conf();"},{"text":"The replica also needs its own certificate and must be reloaded similarly","evidence_ids":["RB-024#2"],"quote":"Yes. auth-db-02 has its own certificate and its own timer."}],"next_checks":["Run the openssl s_client command and compare serial numbers with the file in /etc/postgresql/16/main/server.crt","Execute SELECT pg_reload_conf() on both primary and replica and verify new connections present the updated certificate","Check the pg-cert-renew.timer logs on auth-db-02 to confirm its certificate was renewed"]}
